design_detail: Two-page report in Science (1982) of one rat experiment, run in six replications. Opiate-inexperienced male rats with permanent jugular cannulas received 15 intravenous heroin injections, one every other day, in rising doses (1 mg/kg once, 2 mg/kg twice, 4 mg/kg four times, 8 mg/kg eight times), and a volume-matched injection of the vehicle (5 percent dextrose) on each day between. Injections were given in two settings: the colony, where each rat was individually housed and was taken out of its cage, injected and put back; and a different room with constant white noise at 60 dB SPL, where rats were injected 15 minutes after being carried in and kept for a further 2 hours. One group had heroin in the distinctive room and dextrose in the colony, the other the reverse. All rats were then given a single test dose of 15 mg/kg heroin, either in the setting where they had received heroin (similarly tested, ST) or in the setting where they had received only dextrose (differently tested, DT). A third, control group received 30 daily dextrose injections alternating between the two settings and then the same 15 mg/kg test dose, with no previous opiate experience. The only outcome was death, judged by absence of a heartbeat. Study conditions only; nothing was measured in people.
can_establish: That in these male rats with the same history of escalating intravenous heroin, death after a single 15 mg/kg test injection was about twice as frequent when the injection was given in the setting that had been paired with the vehicle as in the setting that had been paired with heroin, and that both heroin-experienced groups died far less often than opiate-inexperienced controls.
cannot_establish: Anything about people (no human data in this paper); that an unfamiliar place raises overdose risk, since both settings were familiar to every rat and what differed was which one had been paired with heroin; that tolerance was the mechanism (tolerance itself was never measured, only death); how the effect varies with dose, sex, species or route (one dose, male rats, rapid intravenous infusion only); or which features of a setting matter.

sample.recruitment: Laboratory rats; supplier and breeding source not stated (p. 437).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Opiate-inexperienced male rats, Wistar-derived, 90 to 110 days old, cannulated one week before the experiment (p. 437; note 16). No exclusion criteria, no losses and no cannula failures are reported.
sample.demographics: Male only; age 90 to 110 days at the start. Body weights are not reported, although the doses were given per kilogram.
sample.attrition: None reported. Table 1 accounts for 37, 42 and 28 rats; the paper never states the total of 107 (editors' sum).
sample.selection_effects: Not applicable in the usual sense: all animals came from one laboratory and were allocated by the experimenters. How rats were assigned to ST, DT or control, and why the three groups ended up with unequal numbers (37, 42, 28), is not described, so a selection effect cannot be excluded.

exposure.measurement: Doses given by the experimenters through an indwelling jugular cannula at a controlled rate (0.005 mL/s, Harvard model 902 pump), so exposure is known rather than reported by anyone (note 16, p. 437).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. Pretreatment: diacetylmorphine hydrochloride intravenously, 15 injections on alternate days, 1 mg/kg (first), 2 mg/kg (second and third), 4 mg/kg (fourth to seventh), 8 mg/kg (eighth to fifteenth); vehicle on the intervening days. Test: one injection of 15 mg/kg. Solutions were 3.125, 6.250, 12.500, 25.000 and 50.000 mg/mL for the 1, 2, 4, 8 and 15 mg/kg doses, so the infusion lasted about the same time for every rat (about 1 min/kg) (p. 437; note 16).
exposure.polysubstance: None: heroin and 5 percent dextrose only.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: The test dose followed the last pretreatment injection on the usual every-other-day schedule; the exact interval is not stated.

comparison.controls: Two comparisons: ST against DT (same heroin history, different setting at test), and both against a group with no previous opiate experience that had received 30 daily dextrose injections alternating between the two settings (p. 437).
comparison.matching: Same strain, sex and age range; identical pretreatment doses, number of injections and intervals in ST and DT, which the paper emphasises. Setting at test was counterbalanced: of the 37 ST rats, 17 were tested in the distinctive room and 20 in the colony, and half of the 42 DT rats were tested in each setting; the paper states the two counterbalanced conditions did not differ significantly, without giving the numbers (note 17, p. 437).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-exposure measurement of anything: no body weights, no baseline physiology, no measure of tolerance before the test dose. Nothing is known about the rats other than strain, sex and age.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable; control rats received dextrose only before the test dose.

outcomes.instruments: Death after the 15 mg/kg test injection, determined by absence of a heartbeat; time from the start of the injection to death was also recorded (Table 1; note 18, p. 437).
outcomes.validity_norms: Death is an unambiguous outcome; no physiological measure (breathing, blood pressure, temperature, blood concentrations) was taken, so nothing is known about how the rats died.
outcomes.operationalization: Mortality is the percentage of rats in each group that died after the single 15 mg/kg test injection.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported. Three group comparisons and a replication-level test are reported as p values without the test statistics.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Whoever judged death knew which setting the rat was in, because the settings are different rooms.

analysis.effect_sizes: Mortality after 15 mg/kg: ST 32.4% of 37 rats, DT 64.3% of 42, control 96.4% of 28 (Table 1, p. 436). Editors' calculation from those percentages, which fit only one whole number each: 12 of 37, 27 of 42 and 27 of 28 died. DT minus ST is a difference of 31.9 percentage points, a risk ratio of about 1.98 (editors' calculation; 95% interval roughly 1.17 to 3.37 by the Katz log method). Chi-square across the three groups p < .001; both heroin-experienced groups against control p < .002; DT against ST p < .001; in each of six replications a greater proportion of DT than ST rats died, p < .02 by a binomial test (p. 437). No test statistics, degrees of freedom or intervals are printed. Median time from the start of the injection to death: 187 s (ST), 174 s (DT), 164 s (control), described as not significantly different (note 18, p. 437).
analysis.covariates: None. No adjustment for body weight, replication or setting at test.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable in 1982; no protocol or analysis plan is referenced.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only mortality is tabulated. The six replications are not shown separately, the counterbalanced subgroups (heroin test in the distinctive room against the colony) are reported only as 'not significantly different' without numbers, and no test statistic is printed for any comparison.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 37 and 42 rats the difference between 32.4% and 64.3% is estimated with a 95% interval on the risk ratio of roughly 1.2 to 3.4 (editors' calculation), so the direction is reasonably firm and the size is not.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In male rats given the same escalating course of intravenous heroin, a single 15 mg/kg injection killed 12 of 37 (32.4%) tested where heroin had been given before and 27 of 42 (64.3%) tested where only the vehicle had been given before; 27 of 28 opiate-inexperienced control rats died. Deaths occurred within about three minutes of the start of the injection in every group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract proposes a model of overdose deaths in people who use heroin and says the animal results suggest that conditioned drug-anticipatory responses, besides pharmacological factors, affect heroin-induced mortality (p. 436); the body calls the design a methodologically rigorous demonstration of the contribution of contextual stimuli to tolerance (p. 437). The claim about the rats matches the data. The gap is one of framing and of mechanism: a single-dose mortality experiment in 107 male rats is presented as a model of human overdose deaths, with the human background taken from cited sources rather than from any data here, and the explanation offered is a failure of tolerance although tolerance was never measured.

timeline.event: The same group had already reported that the conditioning account of tolerance extends to the harmful effects of very high opiate doses (Siegel, Hinson and Krank, Behavioral and Neural Biology 25, 257), cited here as reference 14
This experiment: heroin at 15 mg/kg killed about twice as many rats when given where the drug had not been given before
The first author's interview series: 10 people formerly dependent on heroin recalled the circumstances of an overdose about 5 years earlier, offered as a check in people of this experiment
The first author's review of drug tolerance and anticipation, restating the account

replication.where_it_stands: No independent replication of this experiment was among the papers read for this card, and no study in people with a comparison group has tested whether the setting of use changes overdose risk. The evidence for the idea in people is one uncontrolled set of ten recollections (Siegel, 1984). The rat finding itself is specific and well defined; what it means for people is untested.

funding.funder: Grants from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada and from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (note 19, p. 437).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated; Science did not require a conflict-of-interest statement in 1982.
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Psychology, McMaster University and University of Western Ontario. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the result.

what_would_settle_it: In people, a case-crossover study of overdose events that compares the setting and circumstances of the overdose occasion with the same person's recent non-overdose occasions, recorded close to the event rather than recalled years later; in animals, an independent replication at more than one dose and in both sexes, with a measure of tolerance (for example respiratory depression) rather than death alone.

domains.note: No method of allocating rats to ST, DT or control is described; the groups are of unequal size (37, 42, 28) with no explanation.
Same strain, sex and age range, and identical pretreatment in ST and DT; body weights and any other baseline measure are not reported, although doses were per kilogram.
All rats were individually housed in the colony; the second setting is the manipulated variable, not housing. How cages were placed and in what order rats were injected is not reported.

domains.domain: 5. Blinding of caregivers and investigators (performance bias)
domains.note: The person injecting necessarily knew which setting the rat was in and whether it had had heroin there; infusion was pump-controlled, which limits what that knowledge could change, but no blinding is reported.
Every rat in each group was assessed for the single outcome.
Death by absence of a heartbeat is hard to misjudge, but who judged it, and whether they knew the group, is not reported; the same applies to the median times to death.
No exclusions, losses or cannula failures are mentioned, and no total is given, so it cannot be told whether every rat entered reached the test.

Only group mortality is tabulated: no test statistics or degrees of freedom for any p value, the six replications are not shown separately, and the counterbalanced subgroups are dismissed as not significantly different without numbers.

The printed p for the main comparison does not reproduce: a chi-square on the Table 1 counts (12 of 37 against 27 of 42) gives about 8.0 and p of about .005, not p < .001 (editors' calculation; the test used is not named).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: SYRCLE defines no overall judgment; this is the editors' summary, set by the worst items that bear on the result. The experiment is simple and its outcome objective, the pretreatment of ST and DT rats was identical by design, the setting at test was counterbalanced, and the effect held in all six replications, which is the strongest part of the evidence. Against that, nothing is reported about allocation, blinding or losses, no test statistic is printed, and the one p value the reader can check does not reproduce from the printed counts. It may be cited for what happened in these rats: roughly twice the mortality when a high test dose was given where the drug had not been given before, and far lower mortality in both heroin-experienced groups than in opiate-inexperienced controls, always labelled as an animal finding. It may not be cited for overdose risk in people, for a 'new place' effect (both settings were familiar), or for the size of the difference as a settled quantity.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Rat, Wistar-derived, male only, 90 to 110 days old, opiate-inexperienced at the start, with a permanent jugular cannula implanted one week before the experiment; 107 rats in three groups (37, 42, 28) (p. 437; note 16).
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Study conditions only. Intravenous diacetylmorphine hydrochloride: 15 injections on alternate days at 1, 2, 2, then 4 mg/kg four times and 8 mg/kg eight times, with vehicle on the days between; then a single 15 mg/kg test injection delivered at 0.005 mL/s (about 1 min/kg) (p. 437; note 16).
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None given. The paper offers no allometric or pharmacokinetic basis for relating these doses to amounts people use, and none should be inferred.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: Only loosely: the escalating schedule imitates rising use and the test dose imitates a large one, but the route (pump-controlled intravenous infusion of a known pure solution), the species, the fixed every-other-day schedule and the absence of any other drug are unlike how people use heroin. Deaths came within about three minutes of the start of the infusion (note 18, p. 437).

key_findings.finding: After a single 15 mg/kg intravenous test dose, 32.4% of 37 rats tested in the setting where heroin had been given before died, against 64.3% of 42 rats tested in the setting where only the vehicle had been given, and 96.4% of 28 opiate-inexperienced control rats.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the printed percentages, each of which fits only one whole number: 12 of 37, 27 of 42 and 27 of 28 rats died.

key_findings.finding: Mortality differed among the three groups (chi-square, p < .001); both heroin-experienced groups survived more often than opiate-inexperienced controls (p < .002); mortality was higher in differently tested than in similarly tested rats (p < .001).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing into the middle column)
key_findings.note: No test statistic or degrees of freedom is printed for any of these. A chi-square on the counts behind Table 1 gives about 8.0 for the last comparison, p of about .005 (editors' calculation); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The experiment was run in six replications, three with testing in each of the two settings, and in every replication a greater proportion of differently tested than similarly tested rats died (p < .02, binomial test).
key_findings.note: Consistent: six out of six in the same direction has a one-sided binomial probability of 0.016 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Both settings were familiar to every rat before the test: each group had received heroin in one setting and the vehicle in the other, 15 times each on alternate days, so the comparison is between a place paired with heroin and a place paired with the vehicle, not between a familiar and an unknown place.
key_findings.note: Recorded explicitly because the finding is often restated as an effect of using in a new place.

key_findings.finding: The setting in which the test dose was given was counterbalanced: of the 37 similarly tested rats, 17 were tested in the distinctive room and 20 in the colony, and half of the 42 differently tested rats were tested in each setting; the paper states the counterbalanced conditions did not differ significantly but gives no numbers.
key_findings.note: Half of 42 is 21 in each setting (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Among the rats that died, the median time from the start of the injection to death was 187 seconds in similarly tested, 174 in differently tested and 164 in control rats, with no significant difference between groups.

Control rats had received 30 daily injections of the vehicle alternating between the two settings and no opiate before the test dose, so the comparison with them is between rats with and without previous heroin, not between settings.

Death, and among the rats that died the time from the start of the injection to death (note 18), were the only outcomes measured: no breathing, blood pressure, temperature or drug concentration was recorded, and tolerance was not measured directly at any point. [The card's own KF5 and outcomes field record the time to death.]

The background figures in the opening paragraphs, that about 1 percent of people dependent on heroin in the United States died each year, mostly from so-called overdose, and that overdose was among the leading causes of death in people aged 15 to 35 in some urban areas, are taken from cited sources of the 1960s and 1970s and are not data from this study.
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the cited sources were not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The p value for the main comparison does not reproduce from the printed table. Table 1 gives 32.4% of 37 and 64.3% of 42, that is 12 of 37 against 27 of 42; a chi-square on those counts is about 8.0, p of about .005 (editors' calculation), while the text prints p < .001. The test used is not named and no statistic is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The difference between the two heroin-experienced groups is still clear and in the same direction in all six replications, but its printed significance is overstated by roughly a factor of five. Cite the counts and the direction, not the printed p.

reporting_issues.issue: No test statistic, degrees of freedom or confidence interval is printed for any comparison: all four statistical statements are bare p values.
reporting_issues.consequence: Nothing but the mortality counts can be checked or re-analysed from the paper, and the precision of the difference has to be computed by the reader.

reporting_issues.issue: The counterbalanced conditions are reported only as 'not significantly different' (note 17), with the group sizes but not the mortality in each setting.
reporting_issues.consequence: It cannot be checked whether the effect held in both directions, that is whether the distinctive room was more lethal in its own right; with 17 to 21 rats per cell such a test would in any case have had little power.

reporting_issues.issue: The three groups are of unequal size (37, 42, 28) and no total, allocation method, exclusion or loss is reported, although every rat carried an indwelling jugular cannula.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether any rats were lost before the test dose, and whether losses differed between groups, cannot be told; the comparison assumes none.

reporting_issues.issue: The explanation offered throughout is a failure of tolerance, but tolerance was never measured: the only outcome is death after a single test dose.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mechanism is an interpretation, not a result. Any claim must say that what was observed was a difference in mortality by setting, not a measured difference in tolerance.
